items.question: Who handed King David’s spears and shields to the commanders?

window_text.9: The commanders of units of a hundred did just as Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each one took his men—those who were going on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off duty—and came to Jehoiada the priest.
window_text.10: Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and that were in the temple of the Lord.
window_text.11: The guards, each with weapon in hand, stationed themselves around the king—near the altar and the temple, from the south side to the north side of the temple.

items.original_question: Who gives the temple weapons to the commanders?

edit.question: Who handed King David’s spears and shields to the commanders?
edit.reason: Identifies the weapons directly and keeps the distinction between their former owner, the giver, and the recipients.

blind.question: Who handed King David’s spears and shields to the commanders?

readings.support: Jehoiada the priest | Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David

assessments.reason: Verse 10 says, “Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields…,” with “he” referring back to “Jehoiada the priest” from verse 9, so the answer matches the key.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly indicates that Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders King David’s spears and shields.

reader.quote:
came to Jehoiada the priest.
10  Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields
reader.contrast: Jehoiada is the giver, while the commanders are the recipients.
reader.reason: The singular pronoun “he” refers to the immediately preceding singular person, Jehoiada the priest; it cannot refer to the plural commanders.

editor.quote:
came to Jehoiada the priest.
10  Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields
editor.contrast: Jehoiada is the giver, while the commanders are the recipients.
editor.reason: The commanders are initially plausible because they dominate the preceding sentence, but “he” refers to the singular Jehoiada, and the commanders are explicitly the people receiving the weapons.

items.question: Who gives the covenant copy to the king’s son?
items.answer: Jehoiada gives the covenant copy to the king’s son.
items.competitor: The king’s son gives the covenant copy to Jehoiada.

window_text.12: Jehoiada brought out the king’s son and put the crown on him; he presented him with a copy of the covenant and proclaimed him king. They anointed him, and the people clapped their hands and shouted, “Long live the king!”
window_text.13: When Athaliah heard the noise made by the guards and the people, she went to the people at the temple of the Lord.
window_text.14: She looked and there was the king, standing by the pillar, as the custom was. The officers and the trumpeters were beside the king, and all the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her robes and called out, “Treason! Treason!”

items.question: Why does Jehoiada say to take the woman out before killing her?
items.answer: Jehoiada says the woman must not be killed inside the temple.
items.competitor: to let the troops kill her followers

window_text.15: Jehoiada the priest ordered the commanders of units of a hundred, who were in charge of the troops: “Bring her out between the ranks and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.”
window_text.16: So they seized her as she reached the place where the horses enter the palace grounds, and there she was put to death.

items.original_question: Why does Jehoiada say to take the woman out before killing her?
items.original_answer: Jehoiada says the woman must not be killed inside the temple.

blind.question: Why does Jehoiada say to take the woman out before killing her?

readings.answer: Because she must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.
readings.support: She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.

assessments.reason: The passage explicitly states, “She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord,” matching the key’s reason that she must not be killed inside the temple.

blind.reason: The text directly gives the reason: she must not be executed in the temple.

reader.quote: “She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.”
reader.contrast: Taking her outside to avoid killing her in the temple, rather than to enable the troops to kill her followers.
reader.reason: The explanatory sentence directly states Jehoiada’s reason for having her brought out. The separate command concerning anyone who follows her does not explain why she herself must be taken outside.

editor.quote: “She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.”
editor.contrast: The reader must distinguish the reason for removing her—avoiding an execution in the temple—from the separate order to kill anyone who follows her.
editor.reason: The explicit “For” clause gives the reason for taking her out before her death. The command concerning her followers is a parallel instruction, not the purpose of removing her.

items.question: Why does Jehoiada make a three-party covenant?
items.answer: So the king and the people will be the Lord’s people.
items.competitor: To post guards at the temple of the Lord.

window_text.17: Jehoiada then made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.
window_text.18: All the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces and killed Mattan the priest of Baal in front of the altars. Then Jehoiada the priest posted guards at the temple of the Lord.

items.original_question: Why does Jehoiada make a three-party covenant?
items.original_answer: So the king and the people will be the Lord’s people.

blind.question: Why does Jehoiada make a three-party covenant?

readings.answer: So that they would be the Lord’s people.
readings.support: that they would be the Lord’s people

assessments.reason: The text says Jehoiada made a covenant "that they would be the Lord’s people"; here "they" refers to the king and the people, matching the key’s meaning.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly states the purpose: that the king and the people would be the Lord’s people.

reader.quote: that they would be the Lord’s people.
reader.contrast: The covenant’s purpose—making the king and people the Lord’s people—versus Jehoiada’s later action of posting temple guards.
reader.reason: The purpose clause directly and completely supports the key. “Three-party covenant” clearly distinguishes the covenant involving the Lord, king, and people from the separate covenant between the king and people.

editor.quote: that they would be the Lord’s people.
editor.contrast: The covenant’s purpose—making the king and people the Lord’s people—versus Jehoiada’s separate later action of posting temple guards.
editor.reason: Posting guards is a later action, not a plausible purpose for making the covenant. The first sentence directly states the covenant’s intended relation, and “three-party covenant” clearly distinguishes it from the following covenant between only the king and the people.

items.question: Why is the city calm?
items.answer: Because Athaliah has been slain with the sword at the palace.
items.competitor: Because all the people of the land rejoice.

window_text.19: He took with him the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards and all the people of the land, and together they brought the king down from the temple of the Lord and went into the palace, entering by way of the gate of the guards. The king then took his place on the royal throne.
window_text.20: All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was calm, because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.
window_text.21: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign.

items.original_answer: Because Athaliah has been slain with the sword at the palace.

blind.question: Why is the city calm?

readings.answer: Because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.
readings.support: because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace

assessments.reason: The reading restates verse 20 verbatim: “the city was calm, because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace,” directly answering the question.

blind.reason: Verse 20 explicitly states the city was calm because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.

editor.quote: the city was calm, because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.
editor.contrast: Athaliah’s death is the cause of the city’s calm; the people’s rejoicing is a parallel outcome, not the stated cause.
editor.reason: The explicit word “because” links the city’s calm only to Athaliah being slain, resolving the plausible alternative that the people’s rejoicing caused the calm.

reader.quote: the city was calm, because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.
reader.contrast: The stated cause of the city’s calm—Athaliah’s death—versus the people’s accompanying rejoicing.
reader.reason: The causal word “because” directly identifies Athaliah’s being slain as the reason the city was calm. The rejoicing is a parallel result, not the stated cause.
